title: Christians, Awake!
description: John Byrom's Christmas hymn "Christians, awake, salute the happy morn" to John Wainwright's tune Yorkshire, in the four parts W. H. Monk harmonized for Hymns Ancient and Modern, arranged for 2 to 4 singers. Verses 1, 2 and 6, in D at the pace the book marks; each verse starts on the low D and climbs three times to a high F sharp.

credits.words: John Byrom (1750), as Hymns Ancient and Modern prints them
credits.arrangement: W. H. Monk's four parts (Hymns Ancient and Modern, 1861), adapted by Stackapella

licence.words: public domain: John Byrom died 28 September 1763 (Julian's Dictionary of Hymnology, as quoted at hymnary.org/person/Byrom_J), and Julian gives 1750 as the earliest date for the hymn; sung here as the Revised Edition of Hymns Ancient and Modern prints it (No. 61, p. 79), verses 1, 2 and 6 of its six, with that book's compilers' wording (their chairman Henry Williams Baker died 1877). The first edition with tunes (1861, No. 47) reads "Whereon the Saviour of mankind was born" (verse 1), "fulfilled" (verse 2), and "To join, redeemed, a glad triumphant throng" and "heaven's" (verse 6), where the Revised Edition has "the Saviour of the world", "fulfill'd", "To sing, redeem'd, a glad triumphal song" and "Heav'n's"; the Revised Edition's capitals ("Angels", "Angelic") are kept. "The Angelic" (verse 2, line 2; verse 6, line 1), eleven syllables to the tune's ten, is sung with "the An-" on one note
licence.tune: public domain: John Wainwright, born about 1723 and buried at Stockport on 28 January 1768 (hymnary.org/person/Wainwright_J; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wainwright_(composer)); the first edition's Index of Tunes (1861, p. xx) gives "Yorkshire", 10 10, 10 10, 10 10, to "Dr. Wainwright"
licence.arrangement: W. H. Monk's four parts for Hymns Ancient and Modern, signed in the first edition's Index of Tunes (1861, p. xx), "Harmonized or Arranged by W. H. Monk", for Hymn 47 (Monk died 1889; public domain): his tune, key and chords as the Revised Edition prints them (No. 61), every part one note a syllable, with the alto and tenor revoiced in a few places for 2 to 4 beginners. The alto takes the third where his alto doubles the tune an octave or a unison lower or sits a fourth under it on a strong beat: F sharp 4 under "Sav-" (verse 1; his A4) and A4 under "of" (his F sharp 4, an octave under the tune's F sharp 5) in line 2; in line 6, G4 under "In-" with the tenor on A3 (his E4 and G3; G4 is his own 1861 alto there), F sharp 4 under "car-" (his D4, an octave under the tune) and A4 under "and" (his F sharp 4). Line 4 opens, under "Which hosts of An-", with the chords of his 1861 printing, since his Revised Edition's F sharp chord on "Which" has its third only in the tenor and the alto can't reach it from the E it holds at the cadence before: A major (alto A4, tenor E4 and bass A2, his 1861 voices; 1875 alto F sharp 4, tenor A sharp 3, bass F sharp 3), then B minor with the bass on B2 as in 1861 (1875 B3, over the bass's beginner range), alto F sharp 4 (his 1861 note) and tenor D4 (his 1861 B3 would move in octaves with the bass), so the duet and trio have each chord's third; then his 1875 chords, with alto E4 and tenor G3 on "of" (his G4 and E4; his tenor E4 is over the tenor's range and a seventh's leap from what goes before) and the alto and tenor exchanged on "An-" (alto D4, tenor B3; his F sharp 4 and D4), so the duet keeps the third of B minor. Under "a-" of "a-bove" his alto's F sharp 4 then E4 is sung as E4 for both beats, the seventh of the F sharp chord falling to D. Breaths written in for beginners: each line's last note gives up a beat, except the song's last. Accepted as printed (verse 1's words; the other verses alike): the song starts with soprano and alto in unison on D; where the tune has A over the bass's F sharp ("lute", "py", "Where-", "a-" of "a-dore", "the" in line 3, "Of" in line 6) his alto sings D, so the duet has root and fifth and the trio's bass gives the third; on "ful" (line 5) his alto doubles the tune's low D for two beats over the bass's F sharp (crossing above the tune would move in octaves with the bass); the duet goes without the third on the weak beats under "iour", "be-" and "nate" and under "a-" of "a-bove", and on the third beats under "them" and "first", where the third is the leading tone C sharp already in the bass, the four-part chords keeping it in the tenor. Also accepted: the tune's top F sharp 5, three single crotchets a verse (the tune spans 16 semitones, so no key keeps it inside the beginner soprano range), and the last line's 10 seconds on one breath, ending on a held "King" a singer may shorten. The tenor's D4, G3, B3 under "hosts of An-" and the alto's fourth up to A4 on "Which", turning back by a third are kept as the price of each chord's third at every size. The printed Amen is left out. "the Angelic" is sung as "th'Angelic", one note for "th'An-", as the 1861 book elides "th' enlightened".
licence.source: Hymns Ancient and Modern for use in the Services of the Church, with Accompanying Tunes, compiled and arranged under the musical editorship of William Henry Monk, Mus. Doc., "The supplemental tunes revised by Charles Steggall", Complete Edition (London: printed and published for the proprietors by William Clowes and Sons, Limited; sold by Henry Frowde, New York; undated, Princeton Theological Seminary Library's stamp 3 June 1921, catalogued 1875), in the Revised Edition's numbering (1875), No. 61, "Christmas", headed "Yorkshire", 10 10 10 10 10 10, with crotchet = 100, p. 78 (its foot marks it "47 Orig. Ed."), in four parts in D major (two sharps), barred in four crotchets, in its printed key here (D); words on p. 79, six verses; read at archive.org/details/hymnsanci00chur/page/n113 (music), n114 (words) and n4 (title page). Checked against the first edition with tunes (London: Novello and Co., 1861), Hymn 47, read from the University of Toronto copy at archive.org/details/hymnsancientmode00unse/page/n83 (words on n84; the Index of Tunes, p. xx, at n25): the tune is the same note for note, and Monk's harmony is the same except in three bars: the first bar of line 4 (1861: A major with alto A4, tenor E4 and bass A2, B minor with the bass on B2, then F sharp over C sharp; 1875: F sharp, B minor with the bass on B3, then C sharp diminished over E), the next bar's first two chords (1861: B minor over D, alto F sharp 4 twice, tenor B3; 1875: B minor over F sharp, alto F sharp 4 then E4, tenor D4) and line 6's second chord (1861 alto G4, 1875 E4)
